meta.title: Who really said "Myths are public dreams; dreams are private myths"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Joseph Campbell wrote it — in Myths to Live By (Viking, 1972). The book says “Myths, so to say, are public dreams”; the internet drops the aside.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Myths are public dreams; dreams are private myths'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Campbell, from Myths to Live By (1972) — not from The Hero with a Thousand Faces, where he phrased the same idea differently.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Campbell wrote it in Myths to Live By, first published by Viking Press in 1972. The sentence sits in a short passage on Freud and reads, in full, “Myths, so to say, are public dreams; dreams are private myths.” The wording that circulates online is that sentence with Campbell’s hedging aside — “so to say” — trimmed out.

docMeta.dd: Essays from lectures at the Cooper Union Forum, 1958–1971
“Myths, so to say, are public dreams; dreams are private myths.”

source.excerpt: Myths, according to Freud’s view, are of the psychological order of dream. Myths, so to say, are public dreams; dreams are private myths.
trail: 1949 — Campbell first states the symmetry in different words in The Hero with a Thousand Faces: “Dream is personalized myth, myth is depersonalized dream,” recorded on Wikiquote ↗ from chapter 1.
1958–1971 — He delivers the lecture series at the Cooper Union Forum that would become Myths to Live By, per the book’s publication record ↗.
1972 — Viking Press publishes Myths to Live By, containing the sentence in its full form; Penguin’s page for the book ↗ reproduces the passage.
17 April 1981 — Campbell says a spoken variant on Bill Moyers Journal ↗: “myth is a public dream and the dream is the private myth.”
source.excerptNote: As reproduced on the publisher’s own page for the book. The popular internet form drops “so to say” and often swaps the semicolon for a comma.

author.name: Joseph Campbell
author.heading: Who was Joseph Campbell?
author.bio: Joseph Campbell (born 26 March 1904, died 30 October 1987) was an American writer and scholar of comparative mythology who taught at Sarah Lawrence College for 38 years, from 1934 to 1972. His The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) argued that the world’s hero stories are variations on one underlying pattern, an idea that later reshaped how Hollywood talks about storytelling. He spent his career pressing a single claim — that myth is not primitive error but the psyche talking to itself in pictures — and this quote is the most compact version of it he ever wrote.

misattribution.heading: What the quote sites get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this really is Campbell. What goes wrong is everything around it: the wrong book, a missing three-word aside, and a habit of welding unrelated Campbell sentences into one fake paragraph.

items.who: The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949)
items.why: The 1949 book contains a different sentence making the same point: “Dream is personalized myth, myth is depersonalized dream” — recorded on Wikiquote ↗ under that title, chapter 1. The public/private phrasing belongs to Myths to Live By, published 23 years later.

Campbell wrote “Myths, so to say, are public dreams; dreams are private myths” — the full sentence is on Penguin’s own page for the book ↗. The hedge is small but it is his; he was paraphrasing Freud, not issuing a slogan.

One Goodreads entry ↗ runs the line straight into “We must be willing to get rid of the life we planned…” and then into a joke about buying a computer, as though the three were one continuous statement. No source is given for the composite, and the three sentences have nothing to do with one another.
AZQuotes ↗ appends two further sentences — “By finding your own dream and following it through…” — and supplies no book, lecture or date for any of it.

misattribution.truthLine: The real sentence is Campbell’s, and it is findable: Myths to Live By (Viking, 1972), where a full-text search of the book ↗ turns up “public dreams” exactly once.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: Campbell was not being poetic for its own sake. He was compressing an argument he had been making since the 1940s: that a myth and a dream are the same kind of object seen at two different scales. A dream is one nervous system working through its own material overnight; a myth is a whole culture doing it across centuries, and neither one is literally true in the way a timetable is true.

The symmetry is what makes it stick. Most attempts to explain myth either flatten it into a lie or inflate it into revelation. Campbell’s sentence refuses both by putting myth and dream on the same footing — which is also, quietly, an argument that your private strangeness is not a defect but a small-scale version of what every culture does.
context.detailsSummary: How the phrasing evolved across Campbell’s career
detailsBody: He had reached for the idea decades earlier in different words. The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) puts it as “Dream is personalized myth, myth is depersonalized dream” — the same symmetry, but built out of clinical-sounding adjectives rather than the plain public/private pair.
Myths to Live By collects talks Campbell gave at the Cooper Union Forum between 1958 and 1971, so the sentence very likely lived as spoken material before it reached print in 1972.

He was still using the formulation late in life. In a Bill Moyers Journal broadcast of 17 April 1981 ↗ — titled, fittingly, Myths to Live By — he said aloud: “myth is a public dream and the dream is the private myth.”
context.pull: A dream is one mind doing overnight what a culture does over centuries.

sourcesVerified.claim: Penguin Random House's official page for Myths to Live By reproduces the passage "Myths, according to Freud's view, are of the psychological order of dream. Myths, so to say, are public dreams; dreams are private myths."

Wikiquote's Joseph Campbell page lists, in its Sourced section under The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949), chapter 1: "Dream is personalized myth, myth is depersonalized dream; both myth and dream are symbolic in the same general way of the dynamics of the psyche." It contains no entry for "public dreams" or "private myths".

Bill Moyers Journal broadcast "Joseph Campbell: Myths to Live By (Part One)", originally aired 17 April 1981, in which Campbell says "myth is a public dream and the dream is the private myth. And if your private myth, your dream, happens to coincide with that of the society, with the mythology of the society, you are in good accord with your group."
A Google Books full-text search of Myths to Live By for "public dreams" returns exactly one result: "Myths, so to say, are public dreams; dreams are private myths."
Wikipedia records Myths to Live By as a 1972 book published by Viking, collecting essays originally given as lectures at the Cooper Union Forum between 1958 and 1971.
Open Library's record for Myths to Live By gives first publication 1972, publisher Viking Press, with a twelve-chapter contents list beginning "The impact of science on myth".
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable 310-page scan of Joseph Campbell's Myths to Live By dated 1972.

Wikipedia gives Joseph Campbell's dates as 26 March 1904 to 30 October 1987, describes him as an American writer, professor of literature and scholar of comparative mythology, and states he taught at Sarah Lawrence College for 38 years (1934-1972).

The Joseph Campbell Foundation's team page states that Michael Lambert manages "the foundation's rights and permissions program, protecting and licensing Campbell and JCF's copyright and trademark material."

Goodreads presents a composite entry welding "Myths are public dreams, dreams are private myths" to "We must be willing to get rid of the life we planned..." and a remark about buying a computer, with no source given.

AZQuotes prints "Myths are public dreams; dreams are private myths. By finding your own dream and following it through, it will lead you to the myth-world in which you live..." with no source or citation.
